newsitem.title: UK: UK TV body says sponsored programme broke codes.
newsitem.headline: UK TV body says sponsored programme broke codes.

text.p: Britain's television watchdog on Wednesday said Carlton Television breached several codes in its broadcast last December of "Now We're Talking," a special programme funded by British Telecommunications Plc.
The Independent Television Commission (ITC) said it issued a formal warning to Carlton over its broadcast of the programme.
The ITC said it "did not accept that an initiative such as BT's Talkworks was an appropriate sponsor for a programme with this theme."

Talkworks is the name of the initiative BT launched in December that was designed to encourage better communication. In addition to funding of the "Now We're Talking" programme, Talkworks has included publication of a booklet on effective conversation and involved sponsorship of Granada Television's "This Morning" programme.

The ITC said the break bumpers, the sponsor credits broadcast during programme breaks on "Now We're Talking", were 14 seconds long, exceeding the 10-second maximum. In addition, the Talkworks brochure offered at the end of the programme was a corporate publication, in breach of codes, the ITC said.

Unlike traditional sponsorship deals that involve financial support from an advertiser for an existing television programme, "Now We're Talking" was advertiser-funded, meaning it was conceived and fully funded by BT, which then approached Carlton with the idea.
"Now We're Talking" marked the first time that an advertiser-funded programme was broadcast during prime time in Britain.
The ITC also said it issued a formal warning to British Sky Broadcasting Group Plc for seriously infringing taste and decency requirements in a broadcast of "Real TV UK" on Sky One on January 7.

The ITC said the programme, broadcast before the 9 p.m. watershed for adult material, included two separate stories in which victims suffered terrible ordeals, including one trapped in a burning car and one attacked by a shark.

Tyne Tees Television was issued a formal warning for breaching codes on protecting the identity of children in sex cases. The ITC said Tyne Tees jeopardised the identify of an alleged child sexual abuse victim in a news report.
